system: You are a helpful assistant. Where the information given does not settle the question, say so and say what would settle it.
message: Our assembly line can only start a production run when parts from all three of our suppliers have arrived. Each supplier independently delivers on time 90% of the time. Our operations director said in the review, with total confidence: "Every supplier is 90% reliable, so we start on time 90% of the time. That's the number we'll quote to the customer." It sounds right to me; they're all at 90%, so the whole chain is at 90%. Can we quote 90% on-time starts to the customer?
response:
**No, quoting 90% would overstate it.** If the three suppliers really are independent, the chance that all three are on time is:

**0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729, or about 73%**

So you'd start late roughly **27% of the time**, not 10%.

### Why the intuition fails
"Each link is 90%, so the chain is 90%" would only hold if the suppliers always succeeded or failed together. Your line needs **all three** to arrive, so any single supplier can delay the start. Each supplier adds its own 10% chance of a delay, and those chances combine.

A quick way to see it: of 100 runs, Supplier A is on time for 90. Of those 90, Supplier B is on time for about 81. Of those 81, Supplier C is on time for about 73.

### What could change the number
The 73% depends on the deliveries being **independent**, which is what you described. In practice that's worth checking:

- **Positively correlated delays** (shared freight carrier, same port, weather, holiday congestion) mean failures cluster on the same days. The real figure would then fall somewhere between 73% and 90%.
- **Independent or unrelated failures** keep it at about 73%.
- **More suppliers** make it worse. Five suppliers at 90% each gives about 59%.

### What would settle it
Don't rely on the per-supplier figures. Pull your **historical production-run records** and count how often all three parts were actually on hand at the scheduled start. That joint on-time rate is the number that matters. A few months of data should give a defensible figure, and it will automatically capture any correlation between suppliers.

### Practical options if 73% isn't good enough to quote
- Hold **safety stock or buffer time** for the least reliable or longest-lead parts.
- Push suppliers toward higher reliability. Getting each to 97% gives about 91% combined.
- Quote the customer a lead time that includes a buffer, instead of a start-date promise built on 90%.

Until you have the historical joint data, I'd quote something closer to 73% (or build in buffer) rather than 90%.
